The Court of Appeal in Abuja has reserved judgement in two separate appeals filed by the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) and its Deputy Director, Kolawole Oluwadare, challenging a judgement awarding N100 million in favour of two officers of the State Security Service (SSS) for Defamation.
A three-member panel led by Judge Danlami Senchi reserved judgement on Monday after the parties adopted their final written addresses. The court said it would communicate a date for delivering its judgement.
The appeals followed a 5 May judgement by the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) High Court, Abuja, delivered by Judge Yusuf Halilu. He awarded N100 million in damages to two SSS officers, Sarah John and Gabriel Ogundele, over publications by SERAP and Mr Oluwadare.
Paul Mgbenwa and Oluwatosin Adesioye represented the appellants at Monday’s proceedings, while Akinolu Kehinde, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), led the respondents’ legal team, according to a report by Vanguard.
In their appeals, SERAP and Mr Oluwadare challenged the trial court’s findings that their publications were defamatory and had identified the respondents.
In a brief filed through their lawyer, Tayo Oyetibo, also a SAN, the appellants raised 24 grounds in the appeal. They argued that the publications did not mention the respondents by name, rank, designation or office, and did not include their photographs.
The appellants maintained that the physical descriptions used in the publications were not unique enough to identify the respondents. They also argued that no independent witness testified that readers understood the descriptions to refer to the two officers.

They further challenged the trial judge’s reliance on his own observation of the respondents in court to establish that the descriptions identified them.
SERAP and Mr Oluwadare also disputed the evidence relied on to establish the alleged harm to the respondents. They argued that claims of suspension, professional injury and psychological distress were not supported by independent documentary evidence.
The appellants also questioned the validity of the first respondent’s witness statement, arguing that it was signed at the lawyers’ chambers rather than before a Commissioner for Oaths.
They maintained that their publications were protected by the constitutional right to freedom of expression and raised defences including justification, qualified privilege and fair comment.
However, the respondents maintained that the publications were capable of identifying them, even though they were not expressly named.
They argued that people familiar with the officers could identify them from the descriptions and circumstances surrounding the publications. They also told the court that a witness had testified that the officers could be identified.
At Monday’s proceedings, Mr Kehinde urged the appellate court to dismiss the two appeals for lack of merit.
The dispute arose from publications SERAP made on 9 September 2024 on its website and X account formerly (Twitter) alleging that SSS officials invaded its Abuja office and harassed a staff member.
The publications linked the development to the organisation’s calls for President Bola Tinubu to investigate corruption allegations at the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited and reverse increases in fuel prices.
The two respondents subsequently sued SERAP and Mr Oluwadare for defamation.
In his 5 May judgement, Judge Halilu awarded them N100 million in damages and ordered SERAP to publish apologies in two national newspapers, on two television stations and on its website.
The judge further awarded N1 million in litigation costs and ordered 10 per cent annual interest on the judgement sum until full payment.
